**Equivalent meanings in different scripts should be nearby without collapsing different meanings together.** Collect paired native-script and Romanized examples, including spelling variation and code-switching. Contrastive training can pull true pairs together while separating meaningful negatives. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)

A Romanized string may have several plausible native-script interpretations. Treat transliteration as an auxiliary view rather than an infallible rewrite, and retain the original input. Multiple valid positive pairs help avoid penalizing legitimate spellings.

**Hard negatives protect distinctions.** Examples differing only in a number, negation, or a similar name should not become indistinguishable merely because their script patterns match. Balance batches by language and script so the majority does not dominate alignment.

Evaluate cross-script retrieval and downstream tasks on held-out domains, dialects, and rare entities. Average similarity is insufficient: a model that maps all related phrases close together may lose the exact distinctions needed for search. Shared representation should support semantic equivalence while preserving task-relevant differences and uncertainty in ambiguous transliterations.

**Technical details and references.**

Collect paired native-script and Romanized examples, including spelling variation and code-switching. Train or adapt a shared encoder with contrastive/translation-ranking objectives so equivalent meanings align while different meanings remain separated. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)

Use transliteration as an auxiliary view, not an infallible preprocessing rule: Romanized strings can be ambiguous and named entities may have several spellings. Include hard negatives, multiple positives, and language/script-balanced batches. Preserve original text for display and auditing.

Evaluate retrieval and task accuracy across dialects, scripts, rare names, and mixed-language inputs, using held-out speakers/domains where applicable. A shared embedding neighborhood should not erase distinctions such as negation or numbers merely to improve average cross-script similarity.
